messages.content: What is the freezing point of water at a pressure of 10 kPa?

function.name: thermodynamics_calculate_boiling_point
function.description: Calculate the boiling point of a given substance at a specific pressure, provided in kilopascals (kPa) or atmospheres (atm). Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

substance.description: The chemical name of the substance for which to calculate the boiling point, such as 'water' or 'ethanol'.

message.content:
At 10 kPa (≈ 0.1 atm) the freezing point of pure water is only a few hundredths of a degree above 0 °C.  
Using the Clausius–Clapeyron relation for the solid–liquid transition of water, the shift in melting temperature is

\[
\frac{dT}{dP}\;=\;\frac{T\,\Delta V}{\Delta H_{\text{fus}}}
\]

with  
* \(T \approx 273\;\text{K}\) (the normal melting point),  
* \(\Delta V \approx -1.9\times10^{-5}\;\text{m}^3\!\!/\text{mol}\) (volume decreases on freezing),  
* \(\Delta H_{\text{fus}} \approx 6.01\times10^{3}\;\text{J/mol}\).

This gives \(dT/dP \approx -8.6\times10^{-7}\;\text{K/Pa}\).  
The pressure difference between 1 atm (101.3 kPa) and 10 kPa is 91.3 kPa, so

\[
\Delta T \approx (-8.6\times10^{-7}\;\text{K/Pa}) \times 91\,300\;\text{Pa}
          \approx +0.08\;\text{K}.
\]

Thus the freezing point at 10 kPa is roughly **+0.08 °C** (about 0.08 °C above the standard 0 °C).  

In practice, this difference is very small, so you can treat the freezing point as essentially 0 °C for most engineering or everyday purposes, but strictly speaking it is slightly above zero.
